title: Discordance among nuclear, mitochondrial, plumage, and vocal differentiation in the Dysithamnus mentalis (Plain Antvireo) complex
content:
ABSTRACT
Limited geographic sampling and discordance between taxonomic characters present major challenges for taxonomy. Biased sampling can misrepresent patterns of geographic variation and genetic structure, while contrasting patterns inferred from different genetic or phenotypic markers may support conflicting taxonomic hypotheses. Here, we address these challenges in Dysithamnus mentalis (Plain Antvireo), a bird species complex with 18 plumage-based taxa distributed across Central and South America. The taxonomy of this complex has long been controversial due to the sparse sampling in prior studies, and recent genetic work added complexity to the problem by revealing discordance between genotypic and phenotypic variation. We integrate genomic and phenotypic data to investigate the population genetic structure and geographic variation of the D. mentalis complex, sampling extensively across its vast range. We find that the D. mentalis complex comprises 12–14 phenotypically distinct populations grouped into 6 distinct nuclear genomic clusters. Mitochondrial variation exhibits a different geographic structure that does not align fully with either nuclear genomic or phenotypic variation. While some genetic and phenotypic clusters align, our results revealed widespread discordance between patterns of variation inferred from different markers. Increased geographic sampling further revealed multiple previously unrecognized hybrid zones, indicating weak premating reproductive isolation between most parapatric populations. However, some lineages exhibit substantial genome-wide differentiation and limited gene flow in contact zones, suggesting some degree of reproductive isolation. Our results offer a redefined understanding of the genetic structure and geographic phenotypic variation of the D. mentalis complex, providing a significant step toward resolving its taxonomy while highlighting areas that require further research, particularly in newly identified contact zones.
